progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From v01: a prokaryote has no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles, and has smaller ribosomes. From v02: what a cell membrane, ribosome and cell wall do in a eukaryote; mitochondria release energy by respiration. From v03: a plant cell's wall resists bursting when water enters. Stage 5 (assumed): DNA carries genes; particles spread out. Not assumed: capsule, peptidoglycan, phospholipid, partially permeable, nucleoid, plasmid, flagellum, pilus.
progression.startsWith: Here's the bacterium from the end of the last video, enlarged. It has no nucleus, no mitochondria, no endoplasmic reticulum and no Golgi body. Yet it releases energy, builds proteins, swims, and copies its DNA, and in ideal conditions some bacteria divide about every twenty minutes. So how does a bacterium carry out every life process without membrane-bound organelles?
progression.stopsAfter: describing, from the outside in, the capsule (slimy, mostly sugars, optional: resists drying out, sticking, hiding from immune cells), the cell wall (peptidoglycan mesh: shape, stops bursting), the cell membrane (phospholipid double layer, partially permeable: controls entry and exit; carries many respiration enzymes, doing the job of mitochondria), the cytoplasm (watery jelly: most reactions, everything suspended; small size means no compartments are needed), the nucleoid (a region with no membrane, holding the circular chromosome: essential genes), plasmids (small separate rings of extra DNA, often resistance genes, copied on their own and shareable; not a copy of the chromosome), ribosomes (smaller than eukaryotic ones, never membrane-bound: make proteins in the cytoplasm), flagella (long tails spun by a motor at the base: movement; optional) and pili (short threads: attachment, and transfer of DNA such as plasmids); and answering how each life process runs without membrane-bound organelles.
progression.nextLesson: preparing a wet mount and finding cell structures under a light microscope (route entry bio-y11-fa1-v05).

teaching.task: *How does a bacterium carry out every life process without membrane-bound organelles?*
teaching.causalExplanation: There are nine parts to know, so let's tour the cell like a map: start outside and work in through the layers, look at what's inside, then come back out to the parts that stick out. On the very outside, many bacteria have a capsule: a slimy layer, mostly made of sugars, wrapped around the cell wall. That slime helps the cell in three ways. It stops the cell drying out, it helps it stick to surfaces, like the film that builds up on teeth, and it can help it hide from immune cells. Not every bacterium has a capsule. Under the capsule is the cell wall. In bacteria it's made of peptidoglycan, a tough mesh of sugar chains joined by short chains of amino acids. You met a wall in plant cells, and here it does the same job with a different material. It gives the cell its shape, and it stops the cell bursting when water moves in. If the wall is damaged, water keeps entering until the cell splits open.

On "enlarged" the "Next" chip fades, the two eukaryotic cells slide off to the left, and y11-prokaryote-cutaway-v1.png grows from the thumbnail to fill the centre left; a grey tag "drawn far larger than real; a few micrometres long". On "no nucleus, no mitochondria, no endoplasmic reticulum and no Golgi body" four small grey organelle chips write in a row beside it (the first two with tiny m5x-cell-protein-synthesis-v1.png crops of the nucleus and b6a-mitochondrion-v1.png), each taking a scribble cross on its word. On "Yet it releases energy, builds proteins, swims, and copies its DNA" the coded JobBoard writes at the upper right, one chip per verb: "release energy ?", "make proteins ?", "move ?", "keep genes ?". On "divide about every twenty minutes" a small coded counter beside the plate ticks 1, 2, 4, 8 with a grey tag "ideal conditions". On the question the heading writes: "How does a bacterium function without membrane-bound organelles?" At most three bright text items. Hold one second.
teaching.understandingCheck: Two exam questions. First. A bacterium lives attached to rocks in a fast-flowing mountain stream, where the rocks sometimes dry out in summer. Identify two structures that would help it survive there, and describe the function of each. Pause here to answer. Second. Bacterium A carries a plasmid with a gene for resistance to an antibiotic. Bacterium B, of the same species, has no plasmid. After the two are grown together, some B cells survive the antibiotic. Describe a plasmid and a pilus, and explain how plasmid transfer could account for this result. Pause here to answer.
